Mr Speaker took the Chair at 2 p.m.

Richard Francis Walls QSO

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Honourable members, I regret to inform the House of the death on
30 October 2011 of Richard Francis Walls QS O, who represented the electorate of
Dunedin North from 1975 to 1978. I desire on behalf of this House to express our sense
of the loss we have sustained and our sympat hy with the relatives of the late former
member. I now ask members to stand with me and observe a period of silence as a mark
of respect for his memory.
Honourable members stood as a mark of respect.

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: Following discussions in the
Business Committee yesterday, I seek leave fo r the suspension for the dinner break to
be delayed to allow for the conclusion of all maiden speeches on all days on which they
are scheduled, from Wednesday, 8 February 2012 to Thursday, 16 February 2012.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Is there any objection to that course of action being followed? There
is none.
Questions for Oral Answer—Transfer of Questions, Effect on Supplementary
Questions

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr
Speaker. Before we get on to the first question, I would like to raise with you in advance
of question No. 11, to allow you to give the matter some thought, a question—and it
will take me a minute to get to it—and it is, effectively, whether the breadth of
supplementary questions is restricted as a result of the transfer of a question.
As I have indicated to your office, there is a degree of concern at the transfer of
question No. 11. We are not asking for the l ongstop provisions that are outlined on page
558 of the third edition of McGee to be brought in—I think those are the ones,
particularly Speakers’ rulings 151/5 and 151/6—because we do not think that
necessarily they apply in this case, although it is  close. I also say that given the fact that
the Government has a right to transfer, we accept there has to be a wording change in
order to make sense of the fact that it is  Mr Foss, and not Mr  Key, answering the
question.
But the quote that is given, which is the basis for the question, says “the vast array of
appointments we make.” The Pr ime Minister indicated that it was the question of who
“we” applies to, when the question was transferred from the Prime Minister, who chairs
the appointments committee and chairs Cabinet, and therefore is responsible, as he has
indicated, for a broad range of appointments.  He, I think, referred to New Zealand Post.
Certainly, he did refer to diplomatic appoi ntments of Mike Moore—an area in which,
Mr Speaker, I am sure you have some inte rest. We could, and were intending to, raise
other appointments, because of the nature of  the quotation, which would be available if
the Prime Minister was answering—for example, the appropriateness of the
appointment of Sir Wira Gardiner to head the consultation process.  What I am seeking
is an assurance from you that Opposition—
168 Points of Order 8 Feb 2012

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Members know they must not interject.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: Is it a point of order?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: It is a point of order that has been raised.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: What I am seeking is an assurance from you that
Opposition supplementary questions will not be  restricted to broadcasting matters and
broadcasting appointments, as a result of the decision of the Prime Minister to transfer
this question.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I appreciate that the issue the member has raised is an issue of
order, and it is an issue that is not uncomm only a matter of concern in this House. But I
think the member must accept that, just as questioners often may try to pin a question to
a certain Minister—maybe the Prime Minist er—and try to apply certain tactics to
achieve that, it is the Government’s responsib ility in terms of whic h Minister answers a
question. That is, I think, accepted, except should—as, and the member has already
alluded to this, Speakers’ rulings 151/5 and 151/6 point out, and as, I think, I have also
reiterated in this House—a question be transferred away from a Minister who was the
only Minister who could possibly have the information necessary to answer that
question. That would be unacceptable. That is also, I think, accepted.
In this case, what thought has to be given to  is if the intent of the questioner was to
ask about appointments, then the primary que stion needs to be fo cused exactly on that,
and it is the reality that the responsible Minister should be the Minister who answers it.
Trying to use a tactic to get at  that process may or may not be helpful. On this occasion
I must rule that I believe that there is no thing untoward in this question having been
transferred to the Minister of Broadcas ting. The question simply asks whether the
Minister of Broadcasting agrees with a statement the Prime Minister made. That is the
question. I will have to listen to the supplementary questions as they arise, but that is the
substance of that question—whether the Mi nister of Broadcas ting agrees with a
statement the Prime Minister made. I realise this  is a difficult issue. I realise that trying
to direct questions where questioners want them directed is not always easy, but my best
advice would be—not that the Speaker should be giving advice—that if the substance of
the question is serious, the question should re ally be based on that substance, and the
responsible Minister has to be the one whom it is addressed to. That is by far the safest
way to get questions answered by the responsible Minister.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr
Speaker. I think you came close but did not quite give the assura nce that we were
seeking, and that is that th e supplementary questions we could make relate to the
appointments the Prime Minister makes, not  the appointments that the Minister of
Broadcasting makes, because that is where the quote comes from.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The issue is the member must now reflect on the question being
asked. The question being asked is whether the Minister of Broadcasting agrees with a
statement made by the Prime Minister. That is al l the question is. I will have to listen to
the supplementary questions as they come up, but that is what the question asks, and the
supplementary questions, obviously, have to relate to why th e Minister of Broadcasting
might agree with the Prime Minister or might not agree with the Prime Minister. But
that is what the question asks.
State-owned Assets, Sales—Effect on Economy
1. DAVID SHEARER (Leader of the Opposition) to the Prime Minister: Does he
stand by his statement in the House yesterday, in answer to Oral Question No 2, that his
8 Feb 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 169
Government is selling assets because “New Zealanders want less debt, more productive
assets, and an economy that is going to function, not a load more debt”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: What I actually said was that one of the
reasons National has 59 MPs and the Labour  Party has very few is “because New
Zealanders want less debt, more productive  assets, and an econom y that is going to
function, not a load more debt, as Phil Goff was promising, and, I have no doubt, David
Shearer is, as well.” I certainly stand by that statement.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Does he believe that his asset sale policy is not about paying off
debt; it is just about not borrowing more?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I think there are a range of reasons why the mixed-ownership
model makes so much sense. It is because I think the companies will perform better, it
is because New Zealand will have less debt, a nd it is because we will have $5 billion to
$7 billion to put into the Future Investment Fund. So there are a variety of reasons to
build out the capital markets, and, of c ourse, there are now approximately 1.8 million
KiwiSaver accounts—mums and dads who want to invest in real New Zealand assets.
Those New Zealanders are dying to invest in New Zealand.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. That was a very precise
question about the repayment of  debt. You might want to ask my colleague to ask it
again. It was a specific question and very narrow, and it was not even addressed.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I will hear briefly the honourable Leader of the House.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: I think it is pretty clear that the order of  the day is a bit of
disruption around this particular series of questions—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! That is a not a point of order.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: No, it is an observation. I apol ogise and I will  withdraw as
well. But to the point of order what I woul d say is simply that the Prime Minister’s
answer in Hansard will bear it out when, I am sure, you read some of that later, as I
know you do, that he gave a range of respons es to the question that Mr Shearer asked.
There is no reason why an assumption should be  made that the strict one prescription
inside the question was what had to be ag reed to—not at all. He asked whether he
believed something.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I accept the point th at the honourable Lead er of the House has
made. The question asked whether a certain reason was the reason for certain actions
taking place and the Prime Minister pointed out that actually there were other reasons as
well. I think that is a perfectly reasonable answer.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Has the Prime Minister read comments by economic commentator
Brian Fallow that the asset sales are certainly not the solution to fiscal problems—in
relation to his last answer?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: How is it fiscally rational to sell assets that Treasury tells us are
earning 15 percent, in order to substitute for debt, which would cost us 4 percent?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: All of that will be clear when  the Budget Policy Statement is
released on 16 February. But in broad terms the cost of funding of debt that would
otherwise have to be incurre d by the country if there we re not the resources coming
from the mixed-ownership model is actually s lightly more expensive than the dividend
return overall. Some years there have be en super-profits earned by State-owned
enterprises, but, in fact, they  are embedded in the future price likely to be paid by
investors.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Could he square his answer to supplementary question No. 1 with
the latest Crown assets portfolio report, which found that  2011 dividends were a record
170 Questions for Oral Answer 8 Feb 2012
for the last 5 years, and that the ener gy companies “have wider benefits to New
Zealand” including “securing New Zealand’s future electricity supply”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I have not seen that report but  I do recall the year where there
probably were the most super-profits, and that  was the year when Meridian Energy sold
Southern Hydro—so a bit like selling 49 percent in an exceptional time.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Would the Prime Minister tell the country what more
“productive assets”, to use his words, he has in mind than those four power companies
he intends to sell to mum and dad investor s who own them already, as the KiwiSaver
account holders own those companies already? What are the more productive assets he
is talking about?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Well, firstly, I think it is an interesting point to recognise what
the Crown balance sheet actually looks like,  because at the moment it sits at $245
billion and over the next 4 years it will ne t increase by a further $22 billion. So New
Zealand mums and dads, as he put it, in 4 years’ time under the leadership of this
Government will have $267 billion.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. My question was very
precise. It asked the Prime Minister to tell the country what the more productive assets
are—in his words—he has in mind for the people who alread y own those power
companies he intends to flog off.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I will hear the honourable Leader of the House.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: This is every question getti ng challenged, which is not a
good circumstance for the House to get itself in to, but I would have thought that if he
was asking the question about what productive assets—

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: No—more productive.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: —mum and dad New Zealanders are going to have—more
productive; whichever way you wa nt to put it—the Prime Mini ster was outlining quite
considerable increases in the assets they are going to have. Perfectly reasonable.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member should not be adding that kind of opinion into a
point of order. But the member asked a bout matters to do with  assets. The Prime
Minister was actually answering in a very rational way about the balance sheet and he
had not finished yet. I think the Prime Mi nister should be give n the opportunity to
finish.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: So firstly, the proposition that the member makes is factually
incorrect and he should know that. It is $267 bi llion in assets, not $245 billion as today.
Secondly, if you want my view, $1 billion bein g taken out of some of these assets and
put into 21 st century schools to educate the future  of our young kids is actually more
important than owning 100 percent of Meridian Energy.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr  Speaker. Now look, I did not
enumerate any figure as to the assets; he made it up himself. The second thing, I asked
for the more productive assets. That means, in a commercial scale of things, what would
be more productive than the 15-plus percent assets of the four power companies—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member is now seeking to debate the matter.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: No.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I apologise to the member; I am  obviously stupid, but if talking
about returns on assets is not debating the matter, then forgive me. But the member
asked a question about the more productive as sets, the Prime Minister answered in
relation to the whole balance sheets and ac tually talked about the assets that are
important to the Government, and he talked  about school assets. That was the Prime
Minister’s answer to the question. It is not for me to judge that answer. It is definitely an
answer to the question.
8 Feb 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 171

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Would the Prime Minister tell us what the commercial rate
of return is for the school assets he proposes for this country?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: There are a number of dividends that come from having
schoolchildren educated in 21 st century schools, and if the member does not know
that—

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I asked him what was
the commercial rate of retur n—not a whole lot of social va luations, but the commercial
rate of return—and I am asking you to make him answer the question.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The member cannot expect an answer to be exactly what he would
like the answer to be. If a member asks a que stion like that, the Minister in answering it
will give what the Minister sees as being a rational answer. I believe the Prime Minister
was giving a rational answer to the questi on asked. Question time is not about members
being able to elicit from Ministers exactly  the answer they want. They ask questions,
and the better the question, the better the answer. That is the way it works. Members
need to think about their questions.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Given his answer to supplementa ry question No. 1, has the Prime
Minister read the Treasury re port that found “lit tle evidence to s uggest privatisation
would significantly improve the financ ial performance of many of the SOE
companies”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes, and where I would draw  some difference of opinion
would be in the potential opportunity of many of these companies. If we go and take a
look at Mighty River Power as a good exampl e, here is a company with world-class
geothermal technology looking to take that to the world.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Why can’t they do that if they’re in Crown ownership?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: We are a capital-strapped Government, so we are not going to
invest in that way, but others might. Inte restingly enough, when that monkey over there
making all that noise was in Government, he was actually proposing they do exactly
that, because he wanted to float the offs hoot subsidiaries on the stock exchange. He
promoted it, but now he is in Opposition, he just goes like this.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Is it his intention for the Crown to indemnify the privatised
companies and shareholders for their losses resulting from Treaty issues?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I think the member clearly demonstrated yesterday he does not
have an answer to who owns water, and today he does not understand the Treaty, which
is a compact between the Crown and Māori.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I think it was a very clear
question about whether it is the Government ’s intention to indemnify those companies
for any losses that they suffer. That was not addressed. In fact, the answer was
offensive.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: The question carried an im plication that, under strict
Standing Orders, would make the question out of order. The Prime Minister’s response
was appropriate, and because he was implyi ng there would be lo sses because of the
Treaty of Waitangi, that is not a factual position at all.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I think we have had enough on this issue. I accept the concern that
the answer was perhaps unnecessarily unhelpful,  but it did actually answer the question
in that the Prime Minister’s answer was ar guing that in fact because the Treaty of
Waitangi is a matter between the Crown and M āori, the Prime Minister would seem to
be arguing that there would not be ther efore losses to private companies as a
consequence. If members think that is not a very good answer, ask the Prime Minister in
even more detail about it; th at is what question time is about. The answer may not have
been the greatest answer, but I am sure th e Leader of the Opposition is capable of
asking further pointed questions to dig into it further.
172 Questions for Oral Answer 8 Feb 2012

items.speaker: Te Ururoa Flavell
items.text: If the Government has the duty of active protection and
upholding Te Tiriti o Waitangi, why would it propose the removal of section 9 of the
State-Owned Enterprises Act, which in effect lets not just investors, but the
Government, off the hook?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: The Government has absolute ly no intention of removing
section 9 from the State-Owned Enterprises Act.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Is the Prime Minister telling th is House that Treasury is wrong,
when in its 2011 Crown Ownership Monitori ng Unit report, it reports that these
companies are earning a total return for the Government of 15 percent per annum on
average over the last 5 years?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No, what I am telling the country  is that the dividend flow is
broadly in terms of the forgone interest payments that would be required if debt was
secured, remembering that the Government will always retain 51 percent or more of
those dividends because of its investment, and that there may be some other super-
profits earned, but they are captured in the value of the company and will be in the
valuations.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: What would the Prime Minister ’s advice be to someone who
received financial advice from an adviser who told them they should sell assets
returning 15 percent in order to pay down debt that cost them 4 percent?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I am not sure about the Prime Mini ster’s ministerial responsibility;
however—

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: I’m seeking an opinion.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I do not want to pr event the Prime Minister from being able to
answer the question where he is asked an opinion.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: If it was like that, I might tell th em not to do it, but that is not
the case, because in this cas e, the value difference the pe rson is talking about is off
some pretty ropey numbers, I might say, to star t off. Just to give you an idea, that same
valuation unit he is talking about moves Solid Energy’s valuation from $475 million in
2007 to $2,954 million in 2008. I know they had a good year, but it was not quite that
good, and, secondly, any other kind of change is implied in the value that would be paid
by shareholders.
Economic Growth—Progress
2. PAUL GOLDSMITH (National)  to the Minister for Economic Development :
What progress is the Government maki ng in implementing its economic growth
agenda?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The Government is
making very good progress in addressing the barriers that prev ent businesses from
getting ahead. Prior to the election we re leased our 120-point economic development
action plan that detailed key steps the Government is taking to build modern, productive
infrastructure, cut red tape, build industries,  innovation, and trade, and build a skilled
workforce. A number of these steps are already complete, and 2012 will be about
further progressing them across all sectors. The agenda is built around the
straightforward premise that if we want mo re and better jobs for New Zealanders, we
need to encourage more businesses to be based here.

items.speaker: Paul Goldsmith
items.text: What are the key determinants of business success, and what can
the Government do about them?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: As I see it, businesses depe nd on a combination of six key
things: ideas and innovat ion to create the busi ness; capital to build the business; access
to raw materials; skilled people; public infrastructure, such as power, broadband, and
transport; and, most importantly, access to markets and customers who want to buy their
8 Feb 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 173
products. The Government can help by making access to the ingredients in any business
plan simple and easier, and that is what our 120-point action plan is aiming to deliver,
so that our businesses have a better platform to compete in the wider world.

items.speaker: Paul Goldsmith
items.text: What barriers to success does the Minister see?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Unfortunately, there are a number of people who lack
understanding and realism about economic gr owth, and who say: “We want jobs, we
want jobs.”, but in the next breath say: “But you can’t do that. You can’t build that here.
You can’t expand that, you can’t explore for that, you can’t inve st in property here, and
you can’t do that.” That is the attitude that made it much harder to pay our way in the
world during the 2000s, and as a result we went into recession before the rest of the
world, in early 2008. We should not offer carte  blanche for any development, but we
need to acknowledge that every time we say no, that has direct consequences in terms of
jobs and growth.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Is the Minister aware that despite National’s 2008 election
promise, the wage gap with Australia has grown substantially since his Government was
elected, whether measured on wages or purchase price parity—[ Interruption]—yes, it
has, Mr Key; and does the absence of refere nce to closing the wage gap with Australia
in the Speech from the Throne, in the Prime Minister’s speech in the Address in Reply
debate, or by National during the recent election mean that his Government has
admitted failure and given up on this promise?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: In regard to the first part of the question, I understand that
the member is incorrect on an  after-tax basis. But, act ually, the member makes an
interesting point. [ Interruption] You either want to hear it, David, or you do not. The
member makes an interesting point when ta lking about growth in  Australia, because
what drives a lot of that grow th are many of the things that  have been turned down here
by the Opposition, right across that side of th e House. I think that inadvertently makes
the point that if you want economic growth, you have to be prepared to let businesses
grow and expand.
Transport Funding—Cost-effectiveness and Return on Investment
3. PHIL TWYFORD (Labour—Te Atatū) to the Minister of Transport: Does the
Government consider it important for its tr ansport spending to be cost-effective and
provide a good return on investment?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Has the Minister read his incomi ng briefing, which shows in figure
10 on page 22 the trend for cost-benefit ratios  of approved State highway projects over
the past few years, and is he concerned with the trend that graph shows of increasingly
poor quality investment?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: Yes, and no.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Can the Minister confirm that in the 2007-08 year, before the current
Government came to power, over 75 percen t of State highway expenditure was on
projects with high cost-benefit ratios, but  by 2009-10 less than 10 percent of State
highway expenditure was on projec ts with high cost-benefit ratios, and is he concerned
by this trend?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: In answer to the back part , no. What I do know is that
if this country had people lik e Mr Twyford around in earlier times, perhaps even in the
Vogel times, this country would still be walking around on dirt tracks.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: At a time when the Government is cutting back spending left, right,
and centre, can the Minister explain why ever-increasing amounts of money are being
spent on State highway projects with ever-lower returns on investment, or will he take a
more sensible and balanced approach than his predecessor, Steven Joyce?
174 Questions for Oral Answer 8 Feb 2012

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: I will agree with him that  my predecessor, Steven
Joyce, was an excellent transport Minister, and I am happy that the standards he set
inside the Ministry of Transport will be continued under my watch. Might I just say that
if benefit-cost ratios were all-important , then you would have to ask why David Shearer
does not support the western ring route in Auckland, because that has a very good
benefit-cost ratio.
State-owned Energy Companies—Financial Returns
4. Dr RUSSEL NORMAN (Co-Leader—Green) to the Minister for State Owned

items.speaker: Enterprises
items.text: What, according to the Crown Own ership Monitoring Unit, was the
average total shareholder retu rn of Genesis, Meridian, Mi ghty River Power and Solid
Energy over the last five years and how does that compare to the average cost of
borrowing to the Government right now?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: The Crown
Ownership Monitoring Unit (COMU) estimates that the weighted average total
shareholder return of the four energy comp anies over the last 5 years is 18.5 percent.
This does include major non-cash items, one -off items, revaluations, and changes in
accounting methodology. It includes, for exampl e, the 521 percent re valuation of Solid
Energy, which the Prime Minister spoke about earlier, and also the $600 million one-off
sale of Southern Hydro. So that figure is unusable. A better summary is the weighted
average dividend yield of the 2007-11 years, which is 4.1 percent. COMU advises that
the average cost of Crown borrowing over the last year is 4.5 percent.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: How is it fiscally rational for the Government to sell assets that
earn 18.5 percent in order to avoid taking on debt that costs around 4 percent?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: I think what the member needs to be clear on is that that is not
a valid comparison. The 18.5 percent include s a whole lot of one-off items, significant
changes in accounting policy in the way that  these valuations are determined, and a
number of non-cash items. So th ese are not strictly comparab le in the way that he is
seeking to present it.

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: Why did the Government’s  Pre-election Economic and
Fiscal Update book the revenue from the a sset sales while not taking into account the
forgone dividends?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: My advice to the member w ould be that I think the best
response to that would be when the Budget Policy Statement is released. I think the
Prime Minister said that would be on 16 February.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Is he saying that he disagrees with COMU when it stated that it
is moving to the use of total shareholder value as the key meas ure of company and
portfolio performance? Is the Government accepting that assessment or is it rejecting it?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: Well, the Government accepts it in the sense that it is moving
towards total shareholder funds, but the numbe r of these years, over 5 years, do not use
methodologies that are exactly comparable. It is inconceivable that  the value of Solid
Energy could go from sort of $475 million one year to nearly $3 billion the next, and
not be attributed to accounting changes.  Over time the measurement of total
shareholders’ funds will become a more comparable figure, but currently the changes in

Local Authorities—Rates Increases over Last Two Decades
5. NICKY WAGNER (National—Christchurch Central) to the Minister of Local

items.speaker: Government
items.text: What reports has he received on how much rates increased nationally in
8 Feb 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 175
the decade since the Local Government Act 2002 and how does this compare to the
previous decade?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: Average rates increased
by 6.8 percent per annum since the big changes were made in a whole series of local
government laws in 2002. In the previous decade, rates increased by an average of 3.9
percent per annum. It is not eworthy that if rates had gone up at the pre-2002 rate,
householders would today be paying $500 a year less in rates and the economy as a
whole would be spending a billion dollars a year less in rates.

items.speaker: Nicky Wagner
items.text: How does the 6.8 percent national average rates increase compare
with other components of the Consumers Price Index over the last decade?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: Rates have gone up by more than any other component of
the Consumers Price Index. The 6.8 percent annual increase in rates compares with a
CPI overall increase of 3 percent, food of 3.8 percent, transport of 2.6 percent, clothing
of 0.1 percent, furniture and appliances of  0.1 percent, and housing costs of 5 percent.
The only cost increase that is nearly as great over the past decade is energy costs, which
have increased by 6.5 percent per annum, alt hough I note that in the last 3 years that
energy price increase, with the reforms ma de by my colleague Gerry Brownlee, has
dropped to just 3.3 percent per year. The Government is working on a package of
reforms for local government to ensure that those ongoing larg e increases do not
continue.

Television, Switch-over to Digital—Going Digital Targeted Assistance Package
7. KANWALJIT SINGH BAKSHI (National)  to the Minister of Broadcasting :
What recent announcements has the Governme nt made on progress towards digital
switchover?

items.speaker: Hon CRAIG FOSS
items.text: Last month I announced details of
the Government’s Going Digital Targeted Assistance Package. To keep watching TV,
all New Zealanders need to go digital by getting FreeView, Sky, TelstraClear, or similar
by the end of 2013. Over 80 percent of Kiwi s have already done so and are already
enjoying more channels, better pictures, a nd new services. However, the Government
recognises that a small group of  people need financial, physi cal, or technical help to
switch over. Our targeted assistance package is focused on those most likely to be in
genuine need, and will directly help elderly people on fixed incomes and people with
disabilities to make the transition to digital television.

items.speaker: Kanwaljit Singh Bakshi
items.text: What are the benefits of the switch to digital television for
New Zealand?

items.speaker: Hon CRAIG FOSS
items.text: As we move further into the digital age, the digital switch-over
will deliver more enhanced reception and be tter picture quality, as well as freeing up
radio spectrum. The total economic benefits from this are estimated to be around $2
billion over 20 years.

Citizenship—Promotion to Migrants
10. MELISSA LEE (National)  to the Minister of Internal Affairs : What recent
steps have there been to promote New Zeal and citizenship as a successful settlement
pathway for migrants?

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: I am pleased to advise that on
Monday His Excellency the Governor-General , as part of his first Waitangi Day
programme, hosted a citizenship ceremony at  Government House in Wellington. I was
delighted to play a part in the event as 24 people from 19 countries became New
Zealand citizens. Having the opportunity to  welcome new New Zealanders who have
chosen to make Aotearoa their home was a fitting way to mark our national day.

items.speaker: Melissa Lee
items.text: Why do people apply for citizenship rather than remain on permanent
residency?

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: Becoming a citizen—[ Interruption] When they are ready!
Becoming a citizen shows that a person has made an indelible commitment to making
New Zealand their home, and it shows the rest  of the world that they are proud to call
themselves a Kiwi. For one 9-year-old boy at Monday’s ceremony, becoming a citizen
means the chance to one day become an All Black. New Zealanders as a group are
intensely proud of our distinct  identity, traditi ons, values, and culture, which are
reflected and bound in the notion of our citizen ship and the rights and responsibilities it
brings with it.

Schools, Class Sizes—Treasury Advice

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: T ēnā koe. No, because
Treasury’s independent observa tion was actually that “Stu dent achievement can be
raised by improving the quality of teaching, … Increasing student/teacher ratios, and
consolidation of the school ne twork, can free up funding that  could be used to support

items.speaker: LOUISE UPSTON
items.text: Seventy-five days ago New Zealand gave
its support to the Rt Hon John Ke y in re-electing Nati onal to office. I want to take this
opportunity to thank the people of the Taup ō electorate for their increased support for
me, and I pledge to continue my hard work in representing them.
National is committed to building a brighter future, where New Zealanders have the
jobs, have the incomes, and have the public se rvices that we all aspire to. We started
this work in 2008, and with an increase in support in the recent election, we are happy
to continue delivering this. One of the four main priorities over th e next 3 years is to
build a more competitive and productive econo my. Really, what that means is growing
our exports. That is the focus. It is very appropriate, coming from the Taup ō electorate,
where the main sources of employment come from farming, forestry, and tourism, that
this is very close to my heart.
Part of our 120-point economic action plan is ensuring that  we sell what the world
wants, but that has to be done at a competitive price, so that is why we have this export-
focused economy. What we know from conve rsations with peopl e up and down New
8 Feb 2012 Address in Reply 185
Zealand is that people want to see more jobs  and they want to se e higher incomes, but
actually we know that those will come from having better international trade links, and
that will lead to a stronger economy and crea te more jobs with higher incomes. That is
one of the fundamental reasons that Ne w Zealanders voted for a National-led
Government.
Part of our strategy around those high-qua lity relationships is with emerging
economies like China and India, as well as our more traditional tr ading partners. We
have had some conversations in the media in  the last few weeks about making the most
of our free-trade agreements and, in particul ar, the one with China. Here in Parliament
today we are recognising the Ch inese New Year, so I felt it important to make sure that
we stress this point of how important they are to us.
One of the things that is important to not e, though, is that this focus needs to be
clearly on the export sector and the tradable sector, because that is where the sustainable
jobs will come from over time. We do not wa nt to see what we saw under 9 years of
Labour, which was an increase in the jobs in the non-tradable sector, so that is clearly
why we have an export focus.
I want to give an example of a company in my electorate, a dairy processing plant
that was opened in August last year, which I took the Prime Minister to in November. It
is called Miraka, which is Māori for milk. It is a really interesting joint venture, because
it combines the M āori landowners with stra tegic partners and inve stors that include the
Māori Trustee, the Global Dairy Network, and the Viet Namese milk and dairy
manufacturing company Vinamilk. Ninety million dollars was invested in the electorate
in this absolutely state-of-the-art milk pr ocessing factory. The two key markets for its
processed goods are customers in Asia and the Middle East. It has been a fantastic
example of a local business that is now em ploying 30 people who would not have been
employed otherwise, as well as $90 million that went into the construction of that milk
processing plant.
But there are some other aspect s of it that I am really excited about, and one of them
is the fact that it is powered by renewable steam a nd electricity from the Tuar ōpaki
Trust’s nearby geothermal power station, whic h is a power station that is owned by the
trust and Mighty River Power. It is even better from an environmental perspective,
because what it also does with its waste water is that it goes on to a neighbouring
farmland, and the solid waste is being disposed of on a worm farm.
This is a business, a local business, a M āori-owned business—54 percent of it
owned by Māori—there is a connection with a State- owned enterprise, it has a fantastic
environmental record, it is exporting our goods to the world, it is employing local
people, and that is exactly what  we want to see more of, not  just in my electorate, but
across New Zealand.
We need investment. In this case, some of it has been foreign investment. Again, it is
something that has been debated at length over the last few weeks, and I was pleased
that our Minister for Economic Development spoke about that more today, because
actually we do not talk enough a bout the benefits of foreign investment. If we continue
to have New Zealanders—as we will for many years to come—demanding higher-
paying jobs, we actually have to look for fo reign investment. That is why it is really
important. [ Interruption] Mr Mallard might think it is not important to have foreign
investment; actually I think th at side of the House has not figured out what their
position is on foreign investment because it seems to change daily or actually several
times a day.
If I look at my electorate, we want to look at foreign inve stment, we want the
opportunities that it brings. Part of it is the sustainability of  the jobs. One of the things
that I love about my electorate is the fantastic ideas that ar e generated, and I have just
186 Address in Reply 8 Feb 2012
given you some examples with the Miraka dairy plant. It is not just  about having ideas
and innovation; it is actually about delivering on those ideas. Whether it is in high-value
wood processing, whether it is alternative us es for geothermal energy—of which there
are multiple examples in my electorate—new farming techniques, creating interesting
trading relationships between nitrogen and carbon, which we have seen in the south of
the Taup ō electorate and which are mitigating envi ronmental issues, or whether it is
software development, we have so me world-leading businesses in Taup ō that are born
out of ideas, and they are exporting from thei r homes, their offices, and their businesses
on the side of our great lake.
This side of the House knows what is impor tant to those indivi duals and to those
businesses, and knows that to get some of  those businesses up and running and off the
ground requires foreign investment. We actually want to encourage them, not
discourage them, which is why I am quite st aggered by the fact that those on the other
side of the House do not s eem that interested in what the advantages of foreign
investment will bring. We want to encourag e those businesses to be based here. We
have to make sure that the resources are av ailable to them, and we  are looking at some
exciting opportunities with geothermal energy. We have got to have the infrastructure
available to them to keep things moving, and we need to ensure that our people have the
right skills and access to capital for them to make it happen.
There is another example in my electorate of  another dairy project that was not quite
so successful, or has not been yet. It had the idea, it had the location, and it was looking
at jobs during construction and jobs during production. It is very exciting for a small
part of my electorate that does not have a lot of jobs cu rrently, and it would be very
helpful to have this sort of opportunity. Un fortunately there have been too many people
who have been opposing it—the location—and r eally slowing the whole process down,
which creates significant issues.
I did want to touch on the Crafar farms very  briefly. For the people of my electorate,
it is an exciting opportunity that  those farms have finally been sold. So instead of the
farms languishing in the hands of the receiver, we will now see investment, we will now
see jobs, we will now see the opportunities that that investment in skills, in training, and
in capital development will provide. It is so  important that that sale means things can
get moving and it means that people in my area can be better off. It was quite
interesting, because we get the odd comment from the other side of the House about
why this was not a good idea. But I think th ey continue to be confused, because we
heard yesterday from David Parker that in 3 years—2006-08—the y had approved four
times what we have approved in only the first term.
It is kind of puzzling, I do not know whether Labour members want new jobs. They
obviously do not want any fore ign investment, or at least they do not in this hour.
Clearly they do not want better environmental practices on farms. We need to encourage
the development of all our opportunities if we are to prosper. This is what will create the
jobs that we want long term. This Governme nt is about less spendi ng, less debt. It is
about more investment, more exports, and mo re jobs. That is what New Zealanders
voted for 75 days ago, and that is what we will deliver.

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: I have been paying quite a bit of attention not only,
obviously, to the Speech from the Throne but  to the Address in Reply speeches that
have come since, and in particular John Key’ s address to this House. I have been left
with one particular question, and that is wh ere has all the aspiration gone? As I recall,
back in 2008 the National Government was absolutely brimming with it, but now today
we are left with some pale imitation ca lled “muddling through”. That is what the
aspiration has been replaced with. It is a hands-in-your-pocket approach to economic
management, and despite that member over th ere saying that they have a 120-point
8 Feb 2012 Address in Reply 187
plan, the average New Zealander is feeling no benefit from that 120-point plan. Instead,
all they feel is the muddling through. So I think instead that it is timely to remind the
National Government of what it is it seems to have forgotten that it promised New
Zealand.
We were told that we should not be tena nts in our own country. Now, from where I
am sitting, it seems to be the Prime Minister  who has been inconsistent when it comes
to his rhetoric and then his policy. There is  no finer example of that than the Crafar
farms decisions, which that member has just touched on. That is the ultimate example of
where decisions are being made that are not  in the best strategic interests of New
Zealanders. We had a local group willing to purchase that significant parcel of land, and
that member, on behalf of her constituents, cl aims that they are happy with the decision
that has been made around the Crafar farms sa le. I would really ques tion that; in fact, I
would like to see a survey of those constituents. Obviously I do not believe that member
is in fact speaking on behalf of those consti tuents involved with Ng āti T ūwharetoa,
because they take a very different perspective on that sale of land.
In Labour we have been absolutely clear , and indeed we were in the election. We
need to start making decisions that allow us to own our own future, particularly when it
comes to these strategic assets. We are not a party against foreign investment; in fact,
we recognise that in New Zealand, because of our poor savings, we cannot afford to
invest in ourselves. When it comes to resear ch and development, in particular, we do
need investment from abroad. But there are clear distinctions between the example that
the member brought up around a strategic milk project and the sale of this strategic
asset. I do not think we could be any clearer.
What else has the National Government told the public of New Zealand since 2008?
Well, we heard that education was key—it was key to aspiration and it was key to
providing opportunities, particularly to our youngest Ne w Zealanders. And what do we
see now? We see now Treasury suggesting that we should have larg er classrooms in
order to improve our education system—

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Larger class sizes.

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: Larger class sizes. And as the member pointed out in
question time, who can name one parent who th inks that that will  improve educational
outcomes for their child? Not only that but th e major platform that this Government
campaigned on around education was to tell 6- year-olds that they  were failing in
primary education before they even started. Now we are going to ignore international
evidence in favour of a coal ition deal by bringing in ch arter schools. That was the
aspiration this Government has delivered in education.
What about the aspiration around buildin g assets? Members in  this House may
remember that John Key said that that was the track we were going to go down. Instead,
we see ourselves paying an extraordinary am ount to sell them, with no guarantee as to
whom. Not only has that sparked a debate abou t the future of the Treaty clause as it
relates to our State-owned enterprises, but  there has not been, unfortunately, enough
discussion about the removal of the social responsibility clause. That Government may
claim that this is a strategic public-private  partnership of sorts —partial privatisation—
but when you remove from any dictate around  the way these assets  are run, anything
that says that we will continue to have a public interest in the way these State-owned
enterprises operate, that is just a private deal . That is privatisation in costume. We have
consistently pointed out to this Government that that is privatisation by any other name.
What about the aspiration that National had to keep families in New Zealand to try to
stem the tide of Kiwis going to Australia? You need only ask members like Parekura
Horomia how many families have been lost on the East Coast and are travelling abroad
for better opportunities. That is because  the wage gap between New Zealand and
188 Address in Reply 8 Feb 2012
Australia has grown by $32 per week since th is Government came into office. How is
that aspirational for New Zealand? Not only has our economic credibility been
downgraded—we are facing an $18  billion deficit—but this Government’s expectations
and aspirations for itself have been downgraded considerably.
I believe it is time New Zealanders asked for what they were promised. It is time
they asked where the better life they were promised by this Government actually is. I
am not talking just about the most vulnerab le New Zealanders—I think their plight is
probably plain for all to see. I am talking about the people in the middle. I am talking
about the 66 percent of the population who earn $40,000 or less per annum, the people
who cannot even save, let alone own their own home. It is time this House
acknowledged that we have reached a tipping point in New Zealand. Gone are the days
when parents believed that they could le ave their children better off than they
themselves were. In those days hard wo rk was enough to get ahead. Poverty did not
have to last for longer than one generation. Those days, sadly, are gone. Now, according
to the Ministry of Social Development’s br iefing for the incoming Minister, two out of
every five children living in poverty are in households where there is a full-time worker.
This is not about just families who are reliant on benefits to survive; this is also about
families who are working every hour they are given and still cannot get ahead, let alone
give their own children a decent start. Where is the aspiration for those families on
behalf of that Government?
We have to also acknowledge that that m eans that choices are being removed from
families. It is no longer a choice for many families as to whether or not one parent
works and one parent remains at home. Choi ces are now being made not necessarily for
their own interest or the interests of their children but out of desperation to survive. It is
time that we strived to give choices back to those families—choices for them to make in
the best interests of their children.
But what has the Government’s response been to the situation we find ourselves in—
this dramatic change in the make-up of th e way New Zealanders are having to operate,
and the fact that many families hold down not just one job and not just two jobs but
multiple jobs to survive? What has its response been? Well, in the last term of
Government we saw an increase in the most  regressive form of taxation we have, and
we now see that families as a result are su ffering because they spend most of their
discretionary income directly on GST. We ha ve seen inflation increase dramatically
while income levels stagnate. We have seen the Government tinker around with the
minimum wage even though the Prime Mini ster himself has acknowledged that he
could not survive on it. So I ask again:  where is the aspiration for New Zealand
families? This is not a Government, I believe , that is in the process of giving hope. A
Government that stands on the sidelines and waits for the trickle-down theory obviously
is not a Government that can offer these New Zealand families much hope. That is
something that we stand against, and in fact, in direct contrast, we think it is time to
tackle these significant issues. It is time to tackle the fact that a full day’s wage can still
equal poverty. It is time to tackle the fact that familie s no longer have many of these
choices.
Instead of relying on a ministerial inqui ry into poverty, which the Government
agreed to because the Māori Party asked for it as part of a coalition deal—and I question
whether it will continue if the M āori Party removes itself fr om this coalition—we want
to see more rhetoric. You will hear this side  of the House talk about higher wages, not
just racing to the bottom; better jobs, not more jobs by one person to make ends meet; a
boat that will go faster, not a boat that we are putting up for sale; and a clean, green,
clever New Zealand to achieve all of that. That is aspirational and that is what the
Labour Party stands for.
8 Feb 2012 Address in Reply 189

items.speaker: Hon Dr PITA SHARPLES
items.text: T ēnā koe, Mr Deputy
Speaker. K āore au i konei inanahi, ng ā mihi o te Pāremata tau hou ki a t ātou, t ēnā
koutou.[Interruption] Huaki i tētahi kura hou i Kawerau, pai tēnā hoki.
[Thank you, Mr Deputy Speaker. I was not here yesterday, so parliamentary New
Year greetings to us all and to you collectively. [Interruption] I was opening a new
school at Kawerau. That was a great event as well.]
Well, the political year has started with the Treaty and M āori issues right up front
and centre stage, right where they belong. Debate is hot; debate is hot over how the
Treaty affects the Government’s plans to pa rtially privatise a number of State-owned
enterprises. Once again the issue of M āori customary interests and rights in fresh water
has come up. The place of the Treaty in our constitution is up for debate, with national
consultations getting under way this year. Meanwhile M āori are working on strategies
for language growth and M āori economic development. Wh ānau Ora is in its roll-out
stage at this time.
The big question, is how do all these things make a di fference for the people of
Aotearoa, who are living in an increasingly divided and polarised society where the rich
are getting richer and more and more fam ilies are struggling to make it through? The
Māori Party is proud to be at th e centre of the action. We have come to Parliament to
represent our constituents’ view s, to take them to Cabinet, fight them through, and to
work with the Parliament, as a whole, to make a difference for New Zealand.
So that leads me to the question of pove rty. We are happy that the Maori Party has
been able to arrange with National a joint Ministerial Committee on Poverty—

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: Can we join you?

items.speaker: Hon Dr PITA SHARPLES
items.text: We will certainly work w ith you. Minister Turia and
Minister English co-chair this committee, a nd I am a member as we ll. We have already
started with Te Puni Kōkiri out there working very, very hard and showing what a good
ministry it is, doing the job.

items.speaker: Hon Parekura Horomia
items.text: That’s right. You’re closing it down. What a disgrace!

items.speaker: Hon Dr PITA SHARPLES
items.text: Oh, rubbish! Parekura, you know that’s not true. In
working with Te Puni K ōkiri, I have already initiated a number of activities in the areas
of housing and housing help, of jobs and training initiatives, and education initiatives.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Cuts.

items.speaker: Hon Dr PITA SHARPLES
items.text: “Developed” is the word. It is in the most early stages
at this time, but it is really quite exciting to see that sections of the community are
prepared to come forward and contribute, although these are still hard times.
So this brings me to Wh ānau Ora—that beautiful, beautiful policy that is so admired
by all the members in th is House. It is so disappointi ng to see the redneck of racism
emerging around Wh ānau Ora. There have been questi ons asked about one family of
some 180 members who received $6,000, which is a fairly meagre amount when we
think of the scale of the tr ansformation that they are commencing. I have to wonder
what motivates a man to cast doubt on the capacity of families  to turn their lives round.
Why would any politician attack wh ānau who are doing the best they can to improve
their situation and, in the long term, redu ce reliance on State dependency, especially
since I have been informed that the member  who raised this issue knows full well that
his partner received sizable remune ration for advising one of those Wh ānau Ora
collectives?

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Sp eaker. I think it has been a long
tradition and a matter that has been reinfor ced a number of times by Speakers that
members’ families are not brought into debate.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: That point of order is uphel d. Can I just also caution the
member that he used a term initially, when he raised this particular matter in his speech,
190 Address in Reply 8 Feb 2012
which could lead to disorder. I let him get away with it because it was not attributed to a
party or an individual, but he did use a wo rd that is unacceptable to attribute to a
member or a party. So I just raise that consciousness with him. Continue, Dr Sharples.

items.speaker: Hon Dr PITA SHARPLES
items.text: What I have seen occurring through Wh ānau Ora is
real change, tangible outcomes that show families taking responsibilities for themselves.
This funding is about whānau transformation. The value in that is priceless.
Transforming the relationship between wh ānau and the State may take a lot of time,
but we cannot continue to waste Government spending on interventions that make no
lasting difference but just create dependency. Wh ānau Ora is about bringing wh ānau
together to collectively plan to improve their well-being. The outcomes that we have
seen are widespread: they span edu cation, employment, health, and social
transformation. We have wh ānau who have looked at ways to address family violence,
others who have focused on rheumatic fever,  and others who have looked at rebuilding
their lives after the Christchurch earthquake. The outcomes for these wh ānau show they
are getting results. They are turning round tr ends which decades of failed Government
funding have been unable to address.
The Māori Party is about creating real transformation in wh ānau, not just propping
up a system that obviously has not worked for our people over the many decades past.
Whānau Ora is the greatest opportunity that we have had to take back responsibility for
ourselves. So why would anyone want to undermine that?
Another major activity that the M āori Party is involved with  and I am involved with
is the constitutional review. This is a review of the constitution of New Zealand, which
will take place over 2 years. There is a panel of about 12 people, led by Sir T īpene
O’Regan and Emeritus Professor John Burrows , and members such as Peter Chin, Dr
Ranginui Walker, Peter Tennent, Professor Linda Tuhiwai Smith, Hinurewa Poutu, Dr
Leonie Pihama, Bernice Mene, John Luxt on, Dr Michael Cullen, and Deborah
Coddington. So those will be the groups, and they will go out over 2 years and hold
meetings with the community. Parallel to this the iwi leaders have set up another team,

items.speaker: Hon SHANE JONES
items.text: Kia ora an ō tātou. This has been a miserable start

one small thing that can be said about Hekia Parata, it is that she has got every prospect
of improving on the dismal record of her predecessor, but that is another matter.
It is very difficult to take the M āori Party members seriously when on one side they
are saying to some iwi leaders “OK, we’ll tr y to find an opportunity for you to buy into
the shares in this sell-off, in this creation of a new economic cast of commercial
mandarins within M āoridom.” That is the first messa ge they are giving. The second
message they are giving is that they did not know about the most signal elements of
Māori jurisprudence—section 9 and the Lo rd Cooke pronouncemen ts of the late
1980s—and they did not realise it  was so important that it should have formed a key
part of their negotiations as they scurried back to the l eather seats of the chauffeur-
driven cars in order to prop up this Gove rnment. That was the second thing. The third
thing was that they have th en turned round and quietly me ntioned to a number of our
leaders “We can’t actually do much. Can you take  the issue to court? We can’t actually
do much.”
There are members in this House who never particularly got on with those four tōtara
trees Sir Tīpene O’Regan, Matiu Rata, Sir Graham Latimer, and Sir Bob M āhuta. I will
put my hand up for having the odd stoush with he  of Irish extraction in the south. But I
will tell you what: those t ōtara trees were a massive contrast to these weak, timid, and
ill-grown pieces of scrub we see representing our people in the Māori Party. If they have
any integrity about the Treaty—

items.speaker: The second thing is
items.text: what is to happen with the functions—and a lot of them are very
