items.speaker: Hon MARYAN STREET
items.text: Thank you, Mr Deputy Speaker, and, first of
all, may I greet you and say happy New Year and welcome back to that position in the
Speaker’s Chair.
The Prime Minister’s speech at the begi nning of a parliamentary session should be
visionary. It should provide leadership. It shou ld provide the outline of a plan that will
navigate this country through some of its mo st difficult years. And yet all of that was
lacking in the speech that came from the Prime Minister late last year.
Our economy has been downgraded twice under this Government’s watch. The
Government’s own forecasts for our economic productivity have had to be downgraded.
We have moved from 4 percent 8 months a go down to 3.5 percent and then down to 3
8 Feb 2012 Address in Reply 197
percent, and I get the distinct impression that  the Government is si mply trying to make
sure that the country is warmed up to the fact that there will be very little growth in the
next 3 years under its stewardship. The Government’s projections are being
downgraded by Treasury in the same way th at our economy has been downgraded by
international agencies under its watch.
I want to address a couple of issues in particular that demonstrate some of the paucity
of leadership that was shown in the Prime Minister’s speech. First of all, we come to the
vexed issue of the sale of St ate assets. This is the only pl an that the Government would
seem to have, and it is one that most New Zealanders do not approve of. Regardless of
the outcome of the election, it is not incons istent to say that although the Government
won the number of seats it did and managed to cobble together a majority, it did not win
the hearts and minds of people over the issue of the sale of State assets. People oppose
this. And why do they oppose it? It is not to  do with xenophobia. It is not to do with
some kind of racism, which the National Gove rnment has latched on to in order to
frighten people away from debating the issu es of ownership and sovereignty in this
country. We will not be deterred from talki ng about sovereignty in this country because
Ministers opposite wish to blacken and besm irch the argument w ith accusations of
racism, which none of us, of course, wish to be  tarred with, because it is not true; we in
this country are not racist by practice or racist by inclination.
But there is no sense in what the Government is planning. The economic sense is not
present. Why would we sell or partially sell State assets that over the last few years have
been delivering double-digit—15  percent—dividends, on averag e, and use that kind of
revenue to pay off debt? If we are going to  pay off debt that comes in at around about
4.5 percent, on average—4 per cent generally for short-term loans, and 6 percent for
long-term loans—if we are going to sell assets that bring us dividends, on average, of 15
percent in order to offset debt that is costing us somewhere between 4 percent and 6
percent, there is no sense.  There is no superior economic  acumen applying here, and
there is no plan for recovery in that proposition.
The other thing that is important about th is asset sales debate—which also goes to
the question of the Crafar farms, which is a di fferent issue, in that that is about private
property—is the underlying theme that makes th is a touchstone for New Zealanders. It
is the underlying point around sovereignty, around ownership, around  control of our
own destiny, and around owning our future. That is the fundamental point.
Can I just say that this is an argument that  is not isolated to New Zealand. It is not
isolated to New Zealand. It is something that New Zeala nders may feel more strongly
about now than they did in the 1980s, because we have seen the effects of the sale of
assets, and not liked them. We have also tuned in to international conversation about the
sale of national assets—and th e sale of land, in particular—that is occurring in
Argentina, in Uruguay, in Brazil, in Hong Kong, and clearly in Australia as well, but in
any number of places around the world, as nations  look to what they can retain control
of in a world that is increasingly globalised.
New Zealand is in a unique position because  of the Treaty of Waitangi, and this is
something that makes our consideration of sovereignty even more pertinent than in
other parts of the globe. We have a Treaty that has been more honoured in the breach
than in the observance, and we are in the pr ocess of righting those historical wrongs. So
how is it that the Government can be so in ept as to foreshadow  the cancellation of
section 9 of the State-Owned Enterprises Ac t and the non-applicati on of the Treaty to
any private investor in State-owned enterpri ses on the eve of Waitangi  Day? Either that
is cynical in the extreme or malicious and wishin g to stir up racial foment, or it is inept.
I do not wish to characterise this Government as malicious, because that is dangerous
198 Address in Reply 8 Feb 2012
territory. If we have a malicious Government, then God help us all. So I will opt for the
inept theory.
It is completely inept that  this Government should have  ignored what happened in
1986—should not have learnt the lessons from Sir Graham Latimer and the M āori
Council in taking the case against a Labour Government at the time, which had not
thought the issue through, to the Privy Council for settlement. As a result of that, one of
the things that came out of it was the Crown Forestry Rental Trust, so that the land
could not be sold out from under the forests, but the forests could be sold. The trees
could be sold, but not the land, because the land and the ownership of it was still in
dispute under the Treaty of Waitangi. What does this Government not understand about
the last 26 years of history that made it provoke such outrage against the Government
on the eve of Waitangi Day?
The Government should be leading. The Government should be providing a vision
for people that we are moving forward as a united country, through difficult times, to a
place where there is more hope, where there is the hope of jobs for young people, and
where there is a hope of family incomes that families can live on. The Government
should be aspirational, which was its code wo rd 3 years ago. Howeve r, it is nothing of
the sort now. The Government should be leading, it should be aspirational, and it should
be visionary. The pity of it is that this Government is none of those.

items.speaker: Hon CHRIS TREMAIN
items.text: I rise to take a call in this
debate, and start by just reflecting on th e economic illiteracy of the Opposition,
particularly in that last speech by the Hon Maryan Street. I do not say “economic
illiteracy” lightly, because what we see agai n and again and again from the Opposition
is a tactic of trying to confuse people around the sale of State-owned assets, and
particularly the return of dividends from energy companies.
So let us reflect on that for a minute, b ecause what the Opposition wants us to do is
to treat as the same—to put into the same barrel—income earned, with revenue from the
sale of power less expenses being that income , and the sale of a large asset, which was
Southern Hydro; a capital sale. The Opposition wants the public to believe that the sale
of an asset, Southern Hydro, when added to  the genuine profit of those companies year
on year, is what now reflects the dividend, and that that is providing a 15 percent return.
Well, that shows exactly the economic illiteracy that we are talking about. They are
two totally different returns, and if that side  of the House wants to include capital sales
into the dividend stream, well, you know, th at shows exactly th e economic illiteracy
that we are talking about. It shows exactly  why the New Zealand public voted National
into Government, and made it very clear that  they did not trust th e Labour Party to be
the governors of this country, to be in the legi slative seat of this country for the next 3
years.
So I suggest that, if you are going to have a debate about State-owned assets, fair
enough. There are no problems with that. We ce rtainly had that in Hawke’s Bay, loud
and clear. However, make sure you tell the public the facts and make sure you are clear
about that, because I believe that the s caremongering and the way you have approached
your politics over the last 3, 6, 9, 12 years is one of the key reasons you find yourself in
that position now.
Mr Deputy Speaker, congratulations on your elevation to the role of Deputy Speaker;
well done. It is a real privilege to be elec ted as a member of Parliament in this
Government, and to have been elected on the platform that John Key laid out clearly
throughout the election process, well in advance of the elec tion. To say that we do not
have a mandate for State-owned assets is, fr ankly, absolute rubbish. That platform was
laid out a year before we went to the polls—a year before we went to the polls.
8 Feb 2012 Address in Reply 199
There were four key platforms that we stood on: responsibly managing the
Government’s finances, building a mo re competitive and productive economy,
delivering better public services , and, of course, one of the key priorities is rebuilding
that beautiful city of Christchurch. These are messages that resonated strongly in my
electorate.
I spent my campaign doing 30 jobs in 30 days. Throughout the period of the last 30
days of the campaign I spent th at time working out there in businesses, for at least a
morning every day. I got to meet all manner of people, many of whom were working in
low-paid and low-skilled jobs. It was a fasc inating experience to spend time with those
30 businesses. I want to thank the people whom  I had the opportunity to work with, and
I reflect on companies like East Coast Lumb er in Wairoa. I worked on the chain at
AFFCO—

items.speaker: Hon Craig Foss
items.text: The pie shop.

items.speaker: Hon CHRIS TREMAIN
items.text: —and in the pie shop in Maraenui. I worked with the
wonderful owners of that shop and talked to  their customers about the future of New
Zealand and of Napier and the Hawke’s Bay. It was an absolutely wonderful
opportunity.
I am proud to be returned to Parliament —it is an absolute privilege—and to see
National lift its party vote majority in Napi er to nearly 7,000. In saying that, I do want
to acknowledge my opposition in Napier, Mr Stuart Nash. He fought a hard campaign,
and I want to acknowledge that. It is a shame, and unbelievably politically illiterate, that
Mr Nash now does not find himself on the Opposition benches of that party over there.
It is a privilege to be back in Parliament , and I am honoured to have the opportunity to
become a Minister in this Parliament.
I want to acknowledge the whips, though. It is a role that I wa s involved with for
about 4 or 5 years. I say to  Michael Woodhouse and Louise Upston that it is a big job
taking on that role of ha lf sergeant major, half pastor of the local church; get into it, go
hard. I also want to acknowledge Rick Bark er for his efforts, and also—not many have
acknowledged him—Darren Hughes, who left this  Parliament in the last term. I thought
he was an outstanding parliamentarian and he  certainly did an ex cellent job in that
whip’s role.

items.speaker: Hon Craig Foss
items.text: Easy, chief.

items.speaker: Hon CHRIS TREMAIN
items.text: Yes, he is going “Easy, chief”, but I did want to
acknowledge that.
With my new ministries, they present a wonderful challenge, and I am looking
forward to that. In fact, when I received th e warrant as a new Minister I almost had a
baptism of water. Coming in on the Wedne sday, it rained down in Nelson on the
Wednesday night and Thursday, and I found my self in my civil defence role down in
Nelson. I want to acknowledge the fantastic job that civil defence did in that flood.
Certainly the mayors down there, Aldo Miccio and Richard Kempthorne, led the
community exceptionally well, and Jim Frater , who was the controller in Nelson during
that flood event, did a superb job. I think that the community of Nelson should be proud
of the efforts of civil defence in res ponse to the flood, and the recovery efforts
thereafter.
Shortly after that, obviously, we had th e 23 December earthquakes in Christchurch.
Again, I went straight down to Christchurch to  be involved with the recovery there, and
to spend a day with people in the community.
To demonstrate that it was a baptism of water, one of my new roles is also within
transport, and we had the event in Tauranga with the Rena coming apart, so I found
myself up in Tauranga having a look at the recovery respons e of Maritime New
Zealand.
200 Address in Reply 8 Feb 2012

items.speaker: Michael Woodhouse
items.text: More than looking. The Minister had his sleeves rolled up.

items.speaker: Hon CHRIS TREMAIN
items.text: Yes. Once again, I just want to acknowledge the efforts
that are going on in Tauranga to make sure that the recovery process works
exceptionally well. Over half the number of  containers have now been removed from
the ship. It is an extremely trying situation that the salvor s are working in, and I think
they are doing an absolutely fantastic job to get us to where we have got to today.
In terms of the two key portfolios, civil de fence and consumer affairs, they are going
to play a small, but key, part in taking the Government’s agenda forward. I want to
reflect on those in the last few minutes that I have in my speech this afternoon. In terms
of civil defence, the key opportunities there are to learn from Christchurch, and there are
a range of reviews, which are being undertaken as I speak, to consider how civil defence
responded to the events in Christchurch—t he two key earthquake events—and how we
worked there. In doing that, we will refl ect on a review of the Civil Defence and
Emergency Management Plan, and look at whether we could have had a better recovery
framework, which could replace the likes of  the Canterbury Earthquake Recovery
Authority in future events.
The other thing we will be focusing on over the next few ye ars is that we have 16
civil defence regions around the country. A capability assessme nt was done of those in
the last couple of years, and there was si gnificant variability amongst those regions. I
want to make sure that the capability in all of the regions is at a level where the civil
defence authorities in each of the regions can adequately come up to the task in a
significant event.
In consumer affairs we have a range of  activities going on, which I am looking
forward to playing a key part in. The Consumer Law Reform Bill has been on the Order
Paper since last year—I acknowledge John Boscawen and Heather Roy, who played
parts in bringing this bill to the Table— and we will be focusing on bringing that law
through. That is the 20 years’ law, which it will be important to change and bring
forward for the country.
I also want to focus on some legislation that Sam Lotu-Iiga has been working hard
on, and, actually, Carol Beaumont on the other side of the House t oo, and that is the
focus on third-tier lending, and th e credit law reform. We are in the process of drafting
legislation around that as I speak. I am ho peful that that will be available for
consideration at the end of February or ear ly March, and then I am going to make sure
that it is well considered before we get it into the House for review. If there is any
borrowing community out there that needs mo re protection, it is the Pacific Island,
Māori, and P ākehā community who depend sometimes on those third-tier lenders. We
want to make sure that there are checks and balances in place to ensure that borrowers
are well protected.
This Government has a bi g plan, a huge economic age nda, and 120 points that we
aim to get into place over th e next 3 years. I am excite d about the future of this
Government, and where we are taking this country. My 30 jobs in 30 days period,
working through the election, got me close to  people who supported this Government. I
am proud of what we are doing, and I am l ooking forward to the ne xt 3 years. Thank
you.

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: I te taha o taku matua, ko Bolton rāua ko Birman
aku waka. I te taha o taku whaea, ko Tākitimu te waka o tana wh ānau whāngai. Ko Te
Whanga-nui-a-Tara te maunga, ko Waingongoro te awa, ko Waim ārama te marae, ko
Taupunga te whare, ko Ng āti Kahungunu ki Heretaunga te iwi. Ko Ng āti Whakaiti rāua
ko Ng āti Kautere ng ā hap ū. Ko Tiakitai te ta ngata, ko Mohi te wh ānau. Ko Anne
Williams rāua ko Burnett Martin aku mātua. Ko Tracey Anne Martin taku ingoa.
8 Feb 2012 Address in Reply 201
He mihi atu ki ng ā atua i hanga i ng ā mea katoa. He mihi atu ki te whaea o te ao, ko
Papatūānuku e takoto ana ki waho. He mihi atu ki t ēnei Whare. T ēnā koutou, t ēnā
koutou, tēnā koutou katoa. E tū ana ahau i raro i te korowai o ō tātou tūpuna.
[On my father’s side, Bolton and Birman are my ships. On my  mother’s side, the
Tākitimu canoe is her adopted family’s canoe. Te Whanga-nui-a-Tara is the mountain,
Waingongoro is the river, Waim ārama is the courtyard, Taupunga is the house, Ng āti
Kahungunu of Hastings is the tr ibe, and the subtribes are Ng āti Whakaiti and Ng āti
Kautere. Tiakitai is the man and Mohi is the fam ily. Anne Williams and Burnett Martin
are my parents, and Tracey Anne Martin is my name.
I acknowledge the gods who created everything, mother Earth, Papat ūānuku lying
out there, and this House. Greetings to you, greetings to you, and greetings to you all. I
stand beneath the cloak of our ancestors.]
Mr Speaker, firstly, can I congratulate you on your reappointment to the Speaker’s
Chair. And I will take this moment to acknowledge this House and to recognise its
importance as a Whare where vital discussions are held and binding decisions are made,
but recognise also that those gathered with in it are no more important than the people
who placed us here, and that all of us collec tively are here to represent the people of
New Zealand.
I will take a moment to pause and to  thank the hundreds of  thousands of New
Zealanders who, through their votes, requested that New Zealand First once again stand
in this House to speak on their behalf. I w ill take a moment to thank the thousands of
party members who never gave up, and who pr ovided, in the final days of our election
campaign, the volunteer assistance that wa s forthcoming from every corner of the
nation. My thanks go to those who gath ered in February 2009 and made the
commitment to keep New Zealand First alive and viable. Their effo rts since that time
have been unsung and unpaid, and we owe them a debt of great thanks.
I will take a moment to acknowledge the leadership of  our rangatira, the Rt Hon
Winston Peters, whose spirit and commitment to the principles of New Zealand First
have led us out of the wilderness and back into Parliament.
I will also take a moment to persona lly acknowledge the s upport of my family,
friends, and community, from those on parent teacher associations and school boards to
kapahaka, Te Wh ānau O Mahurangi, and my respecte d colleagues and staff from the
Rodney Local Board of Auckland Council.
As a sixth-generation New Zealander, my Pākehā ancestors arrived on the Bolton and
the Birman in 1840 and 1842, respectively. You could say that I am returning to my
roots, with the Tonks family having built and operated one of the first brick factories,
flour mills, tram tracks, and blacksmiths shops in P ōneke, now known as Wellington.
Not far from where we sit is the newly rest ored Tonks Grove, with  cottages originally
built by William Tonks for his employees. Even then we believed in good-quality,
affordable housing.
My maternal grandfather and his second wi fe, Maude Mohi, have provided me with
the gift of blood ties to Ng āti Kahungunu of Taupunga marae at Waim ārama in
Heretaunga. My brother-in-law and nieces a nd nephew proudly connect me to the New
Zealand Chinese community, a community whose historical contribution to the building
of our nation is under-repres ented in the pages of our history books. As a wood dragon
baby of 1964, beginning my term in Parliame nt in a water dragon year augers well. I
like to think that in this sink or swim envi ronment this combination gives me a floating
edge. Ji xiang ru yi. Gong xi fa cai.
The birthplaces of my mother and husba nd connect me to the mainland of New
Zealand, and through another brother-in-law our  links stretch out into the Cook Islands.
Kia orana tātou katoatoa i teia ra.
202 Address in Reply 8 Feb 2012
Like many New Zealanders, our family has a proud history of givi ng service to this
nation, with specific mentions of my late gr andfathers, Lieutenant Kenneth Martin, and
his pivotal role at the Featherston pris oner of war camp during World War II before,
during, and after the Featherston riot, a nd warrant officer James Williams, who saw
service in the Egyptian dese rt and Italy as a New Zeal and engineer with the 2 nd New
Zealand Division.
But although I acknowledge being a benefici ary of others’ efforts and struggles, for
me it has been the actions of strong, dete rmined women that cleared the path down
which I walk—women from New Zealand’s pa st, such as Kate Sheppard and Fran
Collett of the press gallery, and strong de termined women from my family’s past:
Martha Anson, Mariah Swaddell, Mary Martin, Beverley Williams, and Maude Mohi.
The last few metres of this particular path have been carved by Anne Martin, continuing
that line of women with character, strength, and quiet wisdom—a woman to whom both
I and New Zealand First owe a gr eat debt. Neither of us woul d be here without her, and
we continue to value her commitment, contribution, and support.
However, while recognising those that made this journey possible, it would be remiss
if I did not acknowledge two men—at least— who are, in very different ways, also
instrumental: firstly, my late father, who held very strong views on many topics and, not
unlike his daughter, expressed them often, but he  also instilled a se nse of personal truth
and loyalty along with a resilience of char acter; and, secondly, my husband. It takes a
very brave man to live with a very strong wo man. As I have explai ned often in recent
days, I am merely part of a team—at home as  well as here in Parliament—and there is
no one’s opinion I trust or value more than  my husband’s. I like to think it was good
planning and exceptionally good taste that landed  me such a man, but, whatever it was,
I am extremely grateful.
To my children—each committee I joined while supporting your growth and
education built on my abilities and helped me gain the confidence required to live by the
motto of Mahurangi College: M āhuhu ki te Rangi, reach for the heavens. From the
playcentre and kindergarten committees, Wark worth School parent teacher association
and board of trustees, and Mahurangi College  board of trustees to kapahaka and Te
Whānau O Mahurangi—they all gave me the c ourage to put my hand up for a bigger
stage. So thank you, my children, for having the good grace to let your mum be all those
things without being so embarrassed you asked her to stop.
For the first 15 of the last 17 years I was a stay-at-home mother. It was not until my
election to the Rodney Local Board of Auck land Council that I re-entered the paid
workforce proper since leaving credit contro l to raise our family. But those who know
me are aware that very little of this time was spent watching The Oprah Winfrey Show
or attending coffee mornings—these are some what of an urban myth to the women I
have had the great pleasure to work al ongside. To those women—the women who are
the backbone of our communitie s, who do for their communiti es as they do for their
families, while many of them also hold down part-time or full-time employment—
please know that you continue to amaze and in spire me. So when a reporter asks me
how I am going to manage my workload with  family and housework, I shake my head
in disbelief and a small amount of amusement because, ladies, it would appear that they
still have no idea what we do on a daily basis. It puts me in mind of the movie Made in
Dagenham. The central character, Rita O’Grady,  is asked by a member of the press
“How will you cope?”. “Cope?”, she respond s, “We’re women. Now stop asking such
stupid questions.”

items.speaker: So to the real question of the moment
items.text: what does a wife, mother, credit controller,
community worker, volunteer, member of the National Council of Women, local
government official, and list member of Parliament sitting on the Opposition benches
8 Feb 2012 Address in Reply 203
do? Well, here is a definition that I believe sums it up: “The opposition, which consists
of all parties not in government, has the role  of holding the government to account. The
opposition usually opposes the government’s policies, questions its actions, draws
attention to issues, promotes alternative policies and debates proposed legislation.”
The Opposition is responsible for challenging the policies of the Government. So that
is my job: to challenge, question, draw attention to issues, debate, and propose
alternatives. Sometimes that might mean a challenge to individual members, such as the
elected members for Helensville and Northlan d. It might be a challenge to work with
those communities and electe d local government representa tives to address the high
social deprivation scores of seven and eight in those electorates; to implement solutions
to the lack of alternative e ducation, access to tertiary or trade education, and high youth
unemployment these communities suffer; and to help those business communities push
forward and gain recognition as  satellite and regeneration to wns, so they can encourage
greater economic development and, through that, employment.
Or it might be to challenge the elected member for Rodney to remember his
verbalised support for the pr ojects of Penlink and the P ūhoi to Wellsford highway with
full retention of access at P ūhoi; to remember north Rodney and that it was a National-
led Government that took it into the amal gamation of Auckland with relatively no
consultation; and to recognise, with the in tended economies of scale that are being
pursued with some vigour, that these communities and businesses find themselves being
starved of tender opportunities and eco nomic development incentives. These
communities and businesses are under stress; they require that member’s attention and
his commitment to truly understand and assist in the solutions to these issues.
Or it might be to challenge this Parliament to recognise that we have done it all
before: we have seen asset sales, we have seen a youth wage, and we have seen a test-
driven education system. Look back—many in th is House were here the last time these
were tried. They did not work then, and they will not work now. The challenge is to
have greater vision and to work to a 100-year view rather than knee-jerk reactions.
I draw the attention of the House to the message of Corinthians 13, verse 11: “When
I was a child, I talked like a child; I thought like a child, I reasoned like a child. When I
became an adult, I put childish ways behind me.” These are not the times for political
games. These are not the times to allow our egos to get in the way of positive solutions
that will benefit our people. These are not the times to  say “I won’t work with that
person or this person.” because we do not lik e their personal style.  These are the times
to act like grown-ups and put away childis h things, because we have all been placed
here to represent our people,  the citizens of New Zealand —not the citizens of Europe,
or Australia, or China, or America, or any other country that comes a knocking. Our job
is to represent New Zealanders first, to get the best deal for New Zealanders first, and to
put the interests and well-being of New Zealanders first.
But, as I close, I also challenge myself . There is another saying that goes “If you
have not done enough to be criticised, then you have not done enough.” My personal
challenge is that by the time I leave this House I hope to be highly criticised.
Āpiti hōno, tātai hōno, te hunga mate ki te hunga mate; te hunga ora ki te hunga ora.
Tēnā koutou, tēnā koutou, tēnā tātou katoa.
[Join and link the descent lines with the dead to the dead, and the living to the living.
Salutations and greetings to each of you collectively and to us all.]

items.text: Honourable members, before I cal l the next member I must say I
